newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Danny knocks out 2.1 bcf US Gulf gas output.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Danny knocks out 2.1 bcf US Gulf gas output.

text.p: Hurricane Danny has forced natural gas producers in the U.S. Gulf to shut in nearly 2.1 billion cubic feet (bcf) per day of production on offshore fields, pipeline operators said Friday.
Danny's path took it straight through some of the richest fields in the country, interrupting about 10 percent of the gas produced in the shallow waters off Texas and Louisiana.
The biggest of the outages was on the Tennessee Gas pipeline system, where the flow of gas gathered in its offshore pipeline system dropped by 600 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd).
Duke Energy said producers cut up to 500 mmcfd of gas through Trunkline and Texas Eastern, two pipeline systems it operates, while Sonat said 380 mmcfd was lost on its systems.
Other outages included about 150 mmcfd cut on the ANR Pipeline system, which was flowing at 825 mmcfd before Danny showed up late Thursday.
Gas moved through the Columbia Gulf pipeline network dropped by 270 mmcfd, while the Transco system lost 100 mmcfd.
A 71 mmcfd outage also was reported on the Stingray Pipeline system.
The storm also caused interruptions on shore, forcing NGC to shut its gas processing plant in Venice, Louisiana.
NGC said the plant, which typically handles about 750 mmcfd, would likely reopen Sunday, but that the closure did not prevent them from routing the gas around the plant.
The volume of gas currently skirting the plant is about 225 mmcfd, reflecting the dwindling flow from evacuated offshore platforms.

Operators started shutting down operations in the path of the storm Thursday, before Danny's maximum sustained winds reached 74 miles per hour, the point at which it graduated from a tropical storm to a force 1 hurricane.
Danny is expected to make landfall some time Saturday along the Mississippi or Alabama coast.

Pipeline companies said there appeared to be little damage from the storm, and most expected the lost production to be restored over the weekend, with some crews returning to platforms as early as this evening.

The interruption to offshore production had little impact on gas prices, but some traders said the combination of record heat this week and the shut-ins could put the industry a bit behind schedule on stock building ahead of the winter heating season.

The New York Mercantile Exchange's futures contract for gas delivered next month at Henry Hub in Erath, La., was down one cent at $2.165 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) at 1500 EDT, just before the market close.
